Hi Dylan,

Thanks for taking this. Quick intro: I'm Jenna (CPO) at Nebula Dynamics. We're evaluating a Dedicated capacity contract with Redwood and need help sizing the GPU mix. High-level workload notes attached (nebula_workload_profile.csv). Key constraints: 32k token context for our main conversational agent, heavy KV-cache reuse, ~8000 embeddings/day (batchable), peak concurrent sessions ~1.2k, soft latency target p50 < 150ms for short-turn prompts and p95 < 800ms for long generation. Cost matters but reliability/SLOs are primary for launch.

Questions:
- For 32k context, do you recommend H100 or A100 as the primary reserve?
- Where does L4 fit (short-turn cheap traffic / embeddings)?
- Any thoughts on reserve vs burst split and fallback routing if H100 capacity is saturated?

We'd like a short call this week to align and then a formal recommendation for procurement. Timeline: procurement starts mid-Oct.

Appreciate your thoughts — attaching the profile.

Best,
Jenna Park
CPO, Nebula Dynamics

Jenna — thanks, got the profile and good summary. Looping in engineering (Irene) and inference sizing (Karthik) to get a rapid recommendation. High-level thoughts so we're aligned for a sync:

- H100 is the safe bet for sustained 32k context with high KV cache fidelity; it gives headroom for long sequences and larger model footprints.
- A100 can be a cost-effective alternative if you shard or split the model to shorter active contexts and rely more on server-side chunking.
- L4 is usually best for embeddings and short-turn cheap queries; great for scale on non-long-context traffic.

I'll schedule a 30-minute call tomorrow. For the recommendation we'll propose a hybrid pool (majority long-context-capable nodes + L4/A100 burst tiers) and include a routing/fallback plan.

Call options: 2026-10-01 16:00Z or 2026-10-01 18:00Z — which works?

Thanks,
Dylan Brooks

Thanks for looping me in. I reviewed nebula_workload_profile.csv and pulled a quick technical read:

Summary observations:
- Active long-context sessions (>=16k tokens) account for ~12% of requests but consume ~48% of token volume.
- Median prompt length is small (~120 tokens) but generation tails extend to 20–30k tokens for some flows.
- KV-cache reuse across turns is high for the same session (>70%), which favors a stable slotting strategy to avoid cache thrash.

Technical recommendations (short):
1) Primary reserve: H100 (8x GPUs)
   - Rationale: H100 has larger HBM and better fp16 throughput for large attention windows; it tolerates larger KV caches and reduces evictions. For a 32k context LLM we avoid repeated reloads which blow latency.
2) Mid-tier reserve/burst: A100 (12x GPUs)
   - Use for mid-length sessions and for overflow when H100 is busy. With careful tiling you can get reasonable throughput with smaller memory footprints.
3) Cheap scale: L4 (20x GPUs)
   - Dedicated to embeddings, short-turn gen, and background batch jobs. L4 is cost-efficient for token-light ops and offers huge scale for embeddings.

Operational notes:
- Slotting: prefer session-affinity binding for long-context users to pin KV caches on H100 nodes. Implement a soft time-to-live (TTL) for pinned slots to free idle caches.
- Batching: continuous batching for embeddings on L4; separate queue to avoid hogging H100 slots.
- Quantization: consider int8/4 for L4 pathways; for H100 stick to fp16 unless you validate quantized accuracy on your eval set.
- Fallback routing: define policy order H100 -> A100 -> L4 (for degraded quality; L4 only for short-turn fallbacks). Include automatic rollback to a smaller model variant if latency/p95 breaches occur.

I've attached a quick cost/perf worksheet (h100_a100_l4_costs_v2.xlsx) with rough tokens/sec and cost-per-token estimates under different concurrency mixes. Also creating a short routing_failover-playbook.md for ops.

I'll follow up with per-GPU throughput numbers and a recommended initial slot count based on your peak concurrent profile.

Irene Choi
Staff Engineer, Inference Runtime
Redwood Inference

Attachment: h100_a100_l4_costs_v2.xlsx (summary: perf profiles, mem headroom, cost/day estimates)

Adding throughput and ops sizing notes. Based on Irene's baseline and Nebula's peak concurrency (~1.2k):

Assumptions used:
- Main model: 20B-ish long-context variant (32k), approx 6.4 GB KV per 1k tokens active window (ballpark; depends on model).
- Short-gen model: 7B for short-turns/low-cost fallback.
- Embeddings: batchable, throughput-friendly.

Initial capacity sketch (reserve + burst hedge):
- H100 reserve: 8 GPUs (target: sustain ~150 concurrent long-context sessions pinned; estimate p50 latency budget met for long jobs if pinned)
- A100 burst-reserve: 12 GPUs (mid-length, can be autoscaled + preemptive burst)
- L4 elastic pool: 20 GPUs (scale for embeddings & short-turns; handle ~10k qps for embedding batch windows)

Why these counts? Balance of cost and SLOs: H100s are expensive but required to keep p95 sensible for 32k sessions. A100s provide cheaper headroom with some tiling and are good for medium-length flows. L4s are the lowest-cost workhorse for non-long-context traffic and bulk embeddings.

Routing policy proposal (short):
- Primary routing: long-context sessions -> H100 (persisted slot)
- Overflow: if H100 observed slot saturation > 80% for 30s, route new sessions to A100 (with notice: degraded max-length)
- Emergency cheap fallback: if both H100/A100 saturated and queue delay > 500ms, route short-turns to L4 with model-size downgrade and user-visible note in payload about degraded fidelity.

Estimated monthly token costs and reserved commitment guidance are in the attached sheet. We should also propose a canary rollout: reserve 4 H100s initially; after 2 weeks of telemetry, scale to 8 if p95 targets not met.

Ops checklist for procurement:
- SLA: 99.9% uptime for primary pool, defined throttling clauses for burst.
- Audit: network egress patterns and KMS policy for keys.
- Support: on-call rotation during initial 4-week ramp.

I'll convert this into a short one-pager for procurement.

Karthik Iyer
Senior Inference PM, Redwood Inference
